extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory, American history, and comparative sociology
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from Tocqueville's Democracy in America analyzing the future condition of Native Americans and the social/political dynamics that affect 'civilization' and survival of indigenous peoples in contact with European settlers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixation and agriculture as prerequisite for civilization
rubrics_metrics.description: “In order to succeed in civilizing a people, it is first necessary to fix it; which cannot be done without inducing it to cultivate the soil; the Indians ought in the first place to have been accustomed to agriculture.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville argues that civilization is rooted in a long process transmitted across generations in the same spot; attempts to diffuse knowledge without settling (e.g., Jesuits in Canada, Puritans in New England) failed because ‘civilization began in the cabin, but it soon retired to expire in the woods.’ Fixing a people to the land and habituating them to tillage is presented as the indispensable preliminary to successful civilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hunter lifestyle impedes acceptance of civilization
rubrics_metrics.description: “Of all nations, those submit to civilization with the most difficulty which habitually live by the chase.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nomadic or hunting peoples vary their dwelling with the animals they pursue and are less able to adopt the regular labor and habits required by agricultural/civilized life; pastoral tribes can migrate more regularly and thus adapt more easily than hunters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural disdain for labor blocks agricultural transition
rubrics_metrics.description: “They consider labor not merely as an evil, but as a disgrace; so that their pride prevents them from becoming civilized, as much as their indolence.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville emphasizes that among many Indians labor is stigmatized (compared to the ox tracing the furrow), and honor attaches to war and hunting. This pride and perception of agriculture as degrading are psychological/cultural barriers to adopting civilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civilization requires gradual internal development rather than external imposition
rubrics_metrics.description: “Civilization is the result of a long social process which takes place in the same spot, and is handed down from one generation to another, each one profiting by the experience of the last.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When knowledge comes from a foreign people while the recipient people are in a position of weakness or subjugation, they rarely assimilate it successfully; successful transitions typically occur by the people’s own gradual efforts rather than sudden transfer from a dominant neighbor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed-race populations accelerate adoption of European habits
rubrics_metrics.description: “The growth of European habits has been remarkably accelerated among these Indians by the mixed race which has sprung up... the half-blood forms the natural link between civilization and barbarism.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville notes that mixed ancestry can transfer intelligence/traits from the colonizing population while retaining some native customs, thereby facilitating modification of savage states and quicker adoption of European manners and institutions (example: Cherokees).

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic competition with settlers undermines native transition to agriculture
rubrics_metrics.description: “When the Indians undertake to imitate their European neighbors, and to till the earth like the settlers, they are immediately exposed to a very formidable competition... The white man is skilled in the craft of agriculture; the Indian is a rough beginner... the Indian has no sooner escaped those evils to which barbarous nations are exposed, than he is subjected to the still greater miseries of civilized communities.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if natives attempt agriculture, they face superior skill, market access, isolation, lack of purchasers, and higher costs, making survival in a settler-dominated economy very difficult and often causing reversion to the wilderness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome of contact depends on balance of power and intellectual preponderance
rubrics_metrics.description: “Whenever the side on which the physical force lies, also possesses an intellectual preponderance, the conquered party seldom become civilized; it retreats, or is destroyed.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville distinguishes cases where barbarians conquer a more civilized people (they may later adopt civilization) from cases where conquerors are both militarily and intellectually superior, producing oppression, loss of land, and cultural extinction for the defeated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relocation promises are unreliable and often lead to further ruin
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal government proposes transporting tribes to remote regions (e.g., Arkansas) at public cost, but Tocqueville warns that such settlements are temporary expedients and that the advance of white populations will track them to new solitudes, leaving their only refuge the grave.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the Union may solemnly guarantee lands and promise protection beyond the Mississippi, Tocqueville argues the government lacks the means to secure them; relocation does not remove the structural pressures (encroachment, economic competition, hostile neighbors) that cause eventual dispossession or extinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal/formal respect vs. de facto rapacity — policy hypocrisy
rubrics_metrics.description: Washington: 'We are more enlightened and more powerful than the Indian nations, we are therefore bound in honor to treat them with kindness and even with generosity.' Yet Tocqueville observes that this high-minded policy has not been followed, and ‘the rapacity of the settlers is usually backed by the tyranny of the government.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal treaties and assurances (articles guaranteeing lands) coexist with state measures and settler actions that effectively dispossess Indians; Tocqueville treats this contrast as a criterion for judging the sincerity and efficacy of government Indian policy.
